title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Saturday morning, Nov 28
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:30 AM ET Saturday, Nov 28, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). The USAID Files query is still the largest and grew overnight (14,732 posts in 24 hours, up from 12,452 last evening) as Republicans rejected a Democratic request to remove files containing personal data; viral posts overstated that request as a demand to pull every file. One new Right claim took off: a false post that Gov. Greg Abbott 'FREEZES Texas certification until a TOTAL statewide audit' matched 6,988 posts (9.34× its prior average, from near zero). Texas's own risk-limiting audit already confirmed Talarico's Senate win, and a federal judge dismissed a hand-count suit (Texas Secretary of State; Texas Scorecard; Democracy Docket). The 'do not certify' slogan jumped overnight (9,228, up from 7,039). On the Far Left, the Van Hollen challenge surged before Tuesday's Dec. 1 vote (9,871, up from 6,357; 6,411 overnight versus 2,892 a night earlier), driven by 'call your senator' posts. The Fetterman–DSCC backlash cooled (1,126, from 1,864). Trump's GDP 'fake numbers' claim faded fast (2,200, from 6,080) and fell from first to ninth. The Hamawy card kept rising (1,606) ahead of his weekend speech; Greenland (2,197) and the KKK claim (1,159) eased. Two faded cards were dropped (Abrego Garcia and the forensic-audit demand). No political topic was on the U.S. trends list. Every count is a query match, not a unique post or user; read the methodology before quoting a number.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The new Abbott card is tagged Right because it casts a Democratic statewide win in Texas as stolen and invents an official action to stop certification. The Hamawy card uses an incoming Democrat's past to brand the new majority as soft on terrorism. The KKK card recasts the party's history to flip racism charges. The Greenland card is a false claim from the President; we tag it Right because it comes from the Republican administration and its supporters, even though on X it spreads mostly through corrections. The Somali card turns Minnesota's fraud cases into a call to remove a mostly citizen community. The GDP card casts the midterm result as the product of 'fake' data. The USAID card casts a past Democratic administration's programs as a censorship operation. The 'do not certify' card casts doubt on elections Democrats won. The Fetterman, Van Hollen and Medicare for All cards are pressure from the party's left on Democratic leaders. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Saturday, Nov 28, 2026, 7:30 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:14 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 27, 5:30 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. All twelve of its narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM ET Friday), so each card also reports its overnight count (5 PM ET Friday to 7 AM ET Saturday) against the same hours a night earlier. Two cards were dropped because they faded: Abrego Garcia (3,314 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.29×; last evening 3,403; 1,259 overnight versus 1,346 a night earlier) and the forensic-audit demand (2,145, 0.28×; last evening 2,514; 1,015 versus 1,384), whose push has moved to the 'do not certify' and Abbott claims. Their fact-checks remain in last evening's snapshot. One card was added with a new query: the Abbott certification-freeze claim. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: posts on Executive Order 13848's Dec. 18 foreign-interference deadline (943 posts, 7.11×; noted on the 'do not certify' card); Schumer plus Israel, AIPAC or Gaza (2,109, 0.76×; noted on the Van Hollen card); and grassroots conservative attacks on Senate GOP leader John Thune over the SAVE Act and the filibuster (1,941, 0.57×; 1,266 overnight versus 380), which is intra-Republican and not an opposition narrative under our definition.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 21, through 7:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 28. The sum is the 'seven-day' total; the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Friday through 7:00 AM ET Saturday) are the 24-hour count; the last 14 hours give the overnight count, compared with hours 25–38 back (5 PM ET Thursday to 7 AM ET Friday). Daily bars are those hourly counts summed by UTC day. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official pages, letters, archives, aggregators, research blogs, X News summaries and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; this morning that includes the Texas Secretary of State's bulletin, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats' letter, Meridian and CryptRing. This morning we researched the new Abbott card and re-researched the USAID, Van Hollen and 'do not certify' cards with fresh post samples; the Greenland and Hamawy cards add a line only; the other cards carry last evening's research and outlet counts and say so. No card topic was on the U.S. trends list.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list when we pulled it. The Abbott, Hamawy and KKK queries had small baselines before this week, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out; a multiple like 20.68× means 'new,' not 'twenty times bigger.' The 'do not certify,' Somali and Medicare for All queries have prior averages inflated by earlier spikes, so their acceleration indexes are low even when they rose overnight. The volume ceiling this morning is 14,732 (the USAID query), up from 12,452 last evening, which lowers every other card's volume index slightly. Read the post counts alongside the scores.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The new Abbott query requires Abbott plus a certification or freeze term plus Texas, Talarico or election, so it catches the many corrections and Grok fact-check replies as well as the claim itself. The other queries are unchanged from last evening and carry the same caveats: the Hamawy query is his surname alone and catches defenders and news relays; the Greenland query catches Danish corrections and unrelated Greenland news; the KKK query catches rebuttals and older history arguments; the GDP query catches news relays and rebuttals; the USAID query catches rebuttals; the Somali query catches Minnesota fraud-case coverage and fact-check replies; the Fetterman query catches primary news; the 'do not certify' query catches rebuttals and other countries' elections; the Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and unrelated 'M4A' uses; the Van Hollen query catches syndicated news. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the Abbott, USAID, Van Hollen and 'do not certify' queries; the other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Abbott FREEZES Texas certification until a TOTAL statewide audit' has no evidence behind it: the Texas Secretary of State said on Nov. 20 that its first statewide risk-limiting audit confirmed the U.S. Senate result with measured risk under 1%, and a federal judge dismissed a suit to block certification pending a full hand count (Texas Scorecard; Democracy Docket). 'Democrats demanded the USAID Files be taken offline' overstates their letter, which asked for removal of files containing personal or sensitive information (CryptRing; Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats). Carried over from earlier snapshots: 'Hamawy has overt ties to terrorists' leaves out context: his work with the Benevolence International Foundation was five weeks of medical volunteering in 1994, eight years before Treasury designated it an al-Qaeda financier, and reporting has not tied him to its al-Qaeda activity; he testified for the defense at the Blind Sheikh's 1995 trial and says he condemns his violence (The Daily Princetonian; New York Post). 'We got Greenland' is inaccurate: Danish officials told Newsweek that the September security agreement the U.S. signed states Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark; it expands U.S. military access, not ownership. 'The KKK was founded by the Democratic Party' is rated False: historians say Confederate veterans founded it in Pulaski, Tenn.; many members were Southern Democrats, but the party did not create it (PolitiFact; AP). On the Somali claims, PolitiFact rated Trump's earlier '92% don't work' figure wrong (about 72% of Somali Minnesotans 16 and older are in the labor force), and IBTimes UK found no data supporting the '2%' figure. 'Only 2% of our Somalian population… have a job… without receiving Government Assistance… The others should be thrown out' has no stated source, and most of the people it targets cannot be 'thrown out': roughly 95% of Somalis in Minnesota are U.S. citizens, most born here, per the state demographer. Somali Minnesotans' labor-force participation (about 72% of those 16 and older in 2024) is above the state's 68%. Benefit use is high (84% received cash aid, food stamps or Medicaid in 2019–2023), so at most about 16% received none — not 2% (New York Post). 'Fake' pre-election GDP: AP reported BEA revises GDP and jobs data on a pre-set schedule 'without regard to the political calendar'; BEA's release attributes the 0.9-point revision to updated software-price and retail data, against a published average advance-to-second revision of 0.5 point. 'GDI killed $200 million in conservative ad revenue' is misleading: GDI's figure is a global, annual estimate of ad money redirected across thousands of sites it rated high-risk (What the Fact). 'Fake economic numbers just prior to the Election' / a 'RECORD SETTING ERROR' is false as stated. BEA released the Q3 revision from 3.4% to 4.3% on its previously announced schedule, not 'three weeks late'; the 0.9-point change was the largest since 2020 but tied for 16th since 1990 and smaller than a 1.2-point revision in Trump's first term (CNBC). Axios reported the claim of a 'purposeful' error was made without evidence; BEA attributed the change to updated software-price and retail-sales data. 'USAID got platforms to defund and deplatform outlets': a review of the release found no USAID award to GDI and no sign its pilot ran (The Media Now). 'Gillibrand is stepping down from the DSCC' is not so: she has said she will seek another term, and the next Senate Democratic leader will name the chair after the Dec. 1 vote (The Hill; The Intercept argued she should be replaced). 'The DSCC endorsed Fetterman' is misleading: Gillibrand said the committee would back him in the general election if he wins the primary, and she did not endorse him in a primary (NBC News; Newsweek; The Philadelphia Inquirer). 'The USAID Files prove USAID got platforms to defund and deplatform outlets' goes beyond the documents: the most-cited item, a 2022 Global Disinformation Index concept note, is a proposal with no budget or award, and no public record shows USAID funded it (DC News Line); Newsweek said it is unclear which proposals were carried out. '38 million invalid voters' is not a finding of illegal votes: the figure's own source, Unite4Freedom, describes the 38 million as 'registrations flagged for further investigation – not 38 million proven illegal registrations,' and we found no official finding that any state's result is in doubt (Democracy Docket; WOWT).

narratives.counter: Don't deny the documents; ask what they actually show. A concept note is a proposal, and GDI's list was a tool advertisers used to decide where to buy ads (The Boston Report). Ask which American outlets were targeted, what USAID actually funded, and whether any post was removed at the government's request. narratives.title: NEW: 'Abbott FREEZES Texas certification until a TOTAL statewide audit' — a false claim spreads on X; Texas's own audit already confirmed Talarico's Senate win
narratives.query: Abbott (certification OR certify OR certifying OR freeze OR froze OR frozen OR freezing) (Texas OR Talarico OR election) lang:en
narratives.sentiment: Cheering in the original post and its copies ('rightfully so!'); in the most-seen replies, corrections dominate — users and Grok replies say no freeze happened
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of posts from 5 PM ET Friday to 7 AM ET Saturday, the top results were corrections: @brianskellenger wrote that Gov. Greg Abbott 'has not frozen Texas certification' and that his news page and the Secretary of State's site show no such order; the pause Abbott ordered this fall was on data-center permits (294 views at sampling). @Haigencut called it 'Not true as framed… invented process claims' (57 views), and more than a dozen Grok replies told users the claim is false. Supportive posts reached fewer people in this sample; X News quoted one: 'Good! At least ONE Governor had stood up to the theft!' Counts are small; this is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: New this morning. A post by @political_rock at 8:34 AM ET Friday claimed 'BREAKING: Abbott FREEZES Texas certification until a TOTAL statewide audit—rightfully so!', said Talarico 'mysteriously rakes in 620,000 MORE votes than Kamala EVER got in 2024' and that '15 MILLION extra midterm ballots' appeared nationwide. The query matched 6,988 posts in the last 24 hours (7 AM ET Friday to 7 AM ET Saturday), 9.34 times its prior daily average of about 748. The busiest hour was 10 AM Friday (675 posts); from 5 PM ET Friday to 7 AM ET Saturday it matched 3,359 posts, versus 6 in the same hours a night earlier. X News summarized the claim overnight. There is no evidence of a freeze. The Texas Secretary of State said on Nov. 20 that the state's first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race met its risk limit in the first round, with measured risk under 1%; of 1,200 sampled ballots, 613 were for Talarico and 494 for Paxton (Texas Scorecard). On Nov. 24, Judge Matthew Kacsmaryk, a Trump appointee, dismissed a Potter County GOP lawsuit seeking to block certification until every paper ballot was hand-counted, calling its claims 'speculation layered on speculation' (Democracy Docket). Talarico's vote total is the one true element: the post compares a midterm Senate race with a 2024 presidential race, and a higher total in a wave year is not evidence of fraud.
talkingPoints: Abbott froze certification until a full audit — finally a governor standing up to the theft.
Talarico got 620,000 more votes than Kamala ever did in Texas. That's impossible.
Fifteen million extra midterm ballots appeared out of nowhere.
Every red state that flipped blue must audit now.
narratives.amplifiers: @political_rock's original post; a TheDonald forum (scored.co) thread that reposted it; reply chains tagging Arizona state Sen. Mark Finchem and @jjauthor; and 'do not certify' reply accounts that attached the slogan to it.
narratives.whyItWorks: It names a real governor taking a decisive action, so it reads like news rather than a demand. Texas really did run new audits this month, and Abbott really did order a pause this fall (on data-center permits), so 'Abbott freezes' sounds familiar. The vote comparison is roughly accurate, which makes the conclusion feel like math. And it gives the 'do not certify' audience a hero in a red state at the moment certification deadlines arrive.
narratives.audience: Texas Republicans stunned by statewide losses; the national 'do not certify' and audit audience; and election-integrity activists who already distrusted Texas's machines and audit rules.
narratives.counter: Point to Texas's own record. The Secretary of State's Nov. 20 bulletin says the statewide risk-limiting audit confirmed the Senate result with measured risk under 1%, and the conservative outlet Texas Scorecard reported it 'supports Talarico win.' A Trump-appointed judge tossed the lawsuit for a full hand count. No order appears from the governor. Comparing a 2026 Senate total with a 2024 presidential total compares different races in different years; wave elections raise totals.

The New York Post (Nov. 26) and the Washington Examiner reported that the incoming New Jersey Democrat is scheduled to speak twice this weekend at American Muslims for Palestine's convention near Chicago, a group sued by the family of Hamas victim David Boim and probed by House and Senate committees. The posts revive his record: in 1994, as a medical student, he spent five weeks volunteering in Bosnia with the Benevolence International Foundation, which Treasury designated in 2002 as an al-Qaeda financier; in the early 1990s he traveled with Omar Abdel-Rahman, the 'Blind Sheikh,' translated for him and testified as a defense witness at his 1995 trial. He's headlining a Hamas-linked group's convention the same weekend.

Keep him off the national security committees.
The NJ GOP let him win without a fight.

Ron DeSantis and NYC Council Member Vickie Paladino. Defenders include reply accounts such as @Cathy2NotToday and supporters who call the scrutiny bigoted.
narratives.whyItWorks: It strings together real, checkable facts — a Treasury-designated charity, a convicted terrorist, a group facing a terrorism lawsuit — and lets the audience fill in the conclusion that Hamawy shares their aims. A fresh news peg (the convention is this weekend) keeps it moving, and it lets the Right recast the Democrats' midterm wave as 'who voters sent to Washington.'
narratives.audience: Pro-Israel conservatives and Jewish voters worried about antisemitism, national-security hawks, New Jersey Republicans, and Republicans looking for a face for the incoming Democratic majority.
narratives.counter: Don't deny the facts; give the context the posts leave out. The BIF work was five weeks of medical volunteering in 1994, eight years before Treasury's designation, and reporting has not tied Hamawy to BIF's al-Qaeda activity (The Daily Princetonian). Testifying as a witness is not support for a crime, and he has condemned Abdel-Rahman's violence. He is a former Army surgeon. Speaking at a convention is not the same as the lawsuit's allegations being proven. Then ask whether the same standard is applied to everyone in Congress.

News relays led the rest: @GlobalNewsHQI's 'TRUMP SAYS: "WE GOT GREENLAND!"… But… America did NOT acquire the island' (2,229 views) and @AnnevanLeur's 'Denmark Hits Back at Trump' (513 views). Last evening's card (Nov. 27, 5:30 PM ET): The query matched 2,750 posts in the last 24 hours (5 PM ET Thursday to 5 PM ET Friday), 1.84 times its prior daily average of about 1,496; 1,470 came from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Friday, versus 110 in the same hours Thursday. The busiest hour was 1 PM Friday (182 posts). After meeting NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago on Thursday evening, Trump told reporters that allies 'weren't very helpful to us on… Iran. But, we got Greenland, and we got Greenland. That's three times the size of Texas, and that made me feel a little bit differently' about U.S. troops in Europe (Newsweek). Danish officials told Newsweek on Friday the claim was 'inaccurate': 'Greenland is part of Denmark. Trump hasn't got Greenland,' and 'the Security Agreement that the US signed states that.' The Sept. 22 agreement, signed by Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic prime ministers, updates a 1951 defense pact: more U.S. activity at Pituffik Space Base and two new defense areas, while affirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination (Newsweek; Hindustan Times; Outlook India). Newsweek said Trump made a similar claim earlier this month on Fox News, when co-host Brian Kilmeade clarified he meant a military agreement. It is tagged Right because it is a false claim from the President; on X it is spreading mostly through corrections.
talkingPoints: We got Greenland — three times the size of Texas.
Trump did what no president could: Greenland is ours.
Europe didn't help on Iran, but Greenland changes the math on troops.
Critics mocked the Greenland push; now look who won.
narratives.amplifiers: Trump's own remarks to the press pool at Mar-a-Lago; MAGA accounts celebrating it. Corrections came from Danish officials via Newsweek, Danish and European users (@Gianl1974, @AnnevanLeur), news relays (@GlobalNewsHQI) and Grok replies.
narratives.whyItWorks: It turns a technical defense agreement into a simple real-estate win with a vivid size comparison, and it links to Trump's long-running Greenland push, so supporters hear a promise kept. Repetition (Fox earlier this month, Thursday again) makes the word 'got' stick even as officials correct it.
narratives.audience: Trump supporters who backed the Greenland push; America First voters skeptical of NATO. The corrections reach Europeans and Trump critics.
narratives.counter: Quote the deal: it expands U.S. military access (Pituffik, two new defense areas) and affirms the Kingdom of Denmark's sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. Denmark's parliament approved it 109–0 on Nov. 19 because it does not transfer the island. 'Access' is not 'ownership' (Newsweek).

factChecks.detail: Danish officials told Newsweek the claim was inaccurate and that the security agreement the U.S. signed states Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Sept. 22, 2026 agreement revises the 1951 defense pact to expand U.S. military access; it does not transfer sovereignty.

talkingPoints: They put out fake economic numbers right before the election to sink Republicans — then quietly fixed them after.
A 'record setting error,' three weeks late: the midterm result was built on rigged data.
The deep state at the statistics agencies picked the winner; investigate now.

narratives.amplifiers: Trump's own Truth Social posts; @GuntherEagleman and copy-paste accounts (@shadygrooove, @Texpatriot26, @wtcrescuer911); @ThePatriotOasis, @ConstitustionX, @JB_Slear. Relayed neutrally by market feeds (@FirstSquawk, @DeItaone per @ClosingPrints) and CNBC.
narratives.whyItWorks: It hands a beaten party a no-fault explanation for the midterm wave: the voters weren't wrong, the numbers were. The revision is real and unusually large, so the claim starts from a true fact, and few people know GDP is estimated three times on a fixed calendar. It came from the President on a holiday, wrapped in a viral, joke-like 'thank you' format that spread as entertainment. And it fits a familiar pattern after Trump's firing of the BLS commissioner last year, so the base already distrusts federal statistics.
narratives.audience: The Republican base looking for an explanation of the midterm losses; election-integrity audiences already sharing 'do not certify' and audit claims; and market-watchers, who saw the post relayed by financial feeds.
narratives.counter: Stick to the calendar. BEA publishes three estimates of each quarter about a month apart; the Nov. 25 second estimate came out on the date announced in advance (CNBC; Axios). The revision was large but not a record — tied for 16th since 1990, and smaller than the 1.2-point revision in 2020 during Trump's first term. The 'fake' pre-election number was already a strong 3.4% that beat forecasts, so it could not have been a plot to make the economy look bad. And BEA sits in a Commerce Department run by Trump's own secretary, Howard Lutnick (Axios).

factChecks.claim: The pre-election GDP figure was 'fake' and its revision should be investigated.
factChecks.detail: AP reported that BEA routinely revises GDP, jobs and other data on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar. BEA's release attributes the 0.9-point upward revision mainly to revised software-price and retail-sales data; its published average advance-to-second revision is 0.5 point.

factChecks.claim: The Q3 GDP revision from 3.4% to 4.3% was a 'RECORD SETTING ERROR' issued 'three weeks late.'
factChecks.detail: CNBC said Trump 'falsely deemed' the revision a mistake: it was released on BEA's previously announced schedule, was tied for 16th-largest since 1990, and was smaller than the 1.2-point revision in Q2 2020.

factChecks.claim: Pre-election GDP numbers were deliberately understated — a 'massive, and purposeful, error.'
factChecks.detail: Axios reported Trump made the allegation 'without evidence'; revisions are routine as fuller data arrive, and BEA explained this one by updated software-price and retail-sales data.
